Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette:
Nabil Haddad was 52 when he came for treatment, a Lebanese American actor who had spent most of his adult life working on sets, in rehearsal rooms, and at public events where being watched was part of the job. Two years earlier, he had been with his wife at a crowded outdoor street festival when a vehicle struck pedestrians at the barricade line. What remained with him was not a smooth story but a series of still images: his wife turning at the sound of children crying somewhere behind them, the metallic crash, a stroller tipped on its side, the frozen look on her face, the bright emergency lights, and later a photograph-like glimpse of her hand on the pavement. He could not make the sequence fully cohere. The memory came in jagged pieces, and each return to it brought a crushing thought that he had failed her, that if he had pulled her back sooner or noticed danger faster she might have lived.

In the months after her death, ordinary sounds became charged. Children crying in a grocery store, sirens or screeching brakes outside his apartment, even news footage of cars plowing through crowds or segments about public safety failures on television could jolt him back into those disconnected snapshots. When that happened, he was overtaken not only by fear and horror but by a renewed conviction that the people meant to protect the public had failed catastrophically and that those responsible had gone on without real consequences. He spoke bitterly about city officials, event organizers, and the security presence that day. He had come to believe that no one had truly been held accountable, and every fresh reminder in the media reopened both the images and the grievance.

Those reminders also altered the way he moved through his days. Because a crying child or the sound of brakes could set off a rush of fear and make his mind splinter into vivid visual fragments, Nabil began arranging his life around not being caught off guard. He stopped going to shopping centers and avoided premieres, theater lobbies, and public festivals where crowds pressed close and escape felt uncertain. At home he kept doors open and the television on in the background because being alone in a quiet room felt dangerous in a way he could not explain to others. If castmates suggested a restaurant after rehearsal, he went along with whatever they wanted rather than risk disagreement or separation from the group; compliance had started to feel like a form of protection.

His sense of threat no longer depended on what anyone told him. Friends, his agent, and even his adult daughter would reassure him that he was safe now, but he found he could not take that in. On set he lost the thread of dialogue during scenes if a child actor cried off camera or if a prop vehicle made a sudden sound. He would become flooded with fear, then angry, then ashamed of how quickly his concentration vanished. In those moments he was certain safety was fragile and unreliable, and that certainty sharpened his attention to the very cues he dreaded. He scanned for noises, for exits, for signs of crowding, which only made the sounds and media stories stand out more vividly.

The more threatened he felt, the more rigid his habits became. He accepted invitations he did not want, lingered in green rooms rather than dressing alone, and let others decide where to sit, when to leave, and how to travel, because any assertion of his own preference felt like risking exposure. Those strategies narrowed his life and, in a painful way, kept his wife’s death mentally close. Staying attached to other people for safety meant hearing more ambient television in waiting areas, more public conversation about current attacks, more unpredictable noise. Avoiding crowds required constant calculation about where crowds might be, and that constant watchfulness made children’s crying and traffic sounds leap out at him. After these episodes, the same visual shards returned, along with the punishing idea that he had not done enough and still was not doing enough.

Over time he began to judge himself through the lens of those precautions. The fact that he could not be by himself in his own apartment without spiraling, or enter a busy event without studying every exit, seemed to him further proof that the world was not safe and that he had been naive before. He also took his own people-pleasing as evidence of moral failure: if he now went along with whatever others wanted just to feel protected, maybe he had always been too passive, the kind of husband who would miss the moment when action was needed. That belief deepened the guilt already attached to the memory and left him even more keyed up.

What finally brought Nabil in was a recent audition for a streaming series. In the waiting area, a child in the hall began to cry while a monitor played muted news footage of a vehicle incident. He lost focus, saw his wife’s hand on the pavement as sharply as if it were in front of him, and had to leave before reading. He told the clinician that he was afraid he was becoming impossible to work with and impossible to live as, a man organized entirely around not being alone and not being surprised. More than anything, he feared that if he let go of his vigilance, he would be failing his wife again; but he also said, quietly, that he wanted some way to remember her without being dragged back into those frozen images every time the world made a familiar sound.
